description: We are AUK Students, this is our third NASA Hackathon as well.
summary:
RIWA Space Journey is a free browser game in which you design, build and fly your own space mission (either solo or with up to three friends). You start off with an empty assembly stand and pick your mission objective, then go on to build your spacecraft piece by piece. You then select your orbit and your rocket and have to keep mass, power, money, data, comms and time in check. You then do your own ground tests, launch and fly for years of operations (things break and you have to read the telemetry to work out why). A report is generated which scores your mission out of 1000 and explains all the results so you can make one change and fly again.

Students very rarely get to actually go through a full mission so the trade-offs are all abstract. In this case every number is derived from real physics (Kepler orbits, solar power, link budgets, the rocket equation) and real NASA data. 13,482 Landsat 8 and 9 scenes determines how often the camera gets a clear view of Angola month on month. Six missions run from a first CubeSat all the way to a crew around the Moon, with 5 levels from Guided (no space knowledge required) to Expert and actual team roles as you would have in a real concurrent design room. It works in any browser so any classroom can play.
details:
RIWA Space Journey is a mission design game for the challenge "Space Mission Design Game". It runs in any web browser (a laptop, a classroom TV or a phone), it's free, and there's nothing to install or sign up for. One mission goes from idea to final report:

  1. Pick a mission and a level, then read the brief: who the mission is for and what they need.
  2. Build the spacecraft from an empty stand, part by part, at five desks (mission, spacecraft, payload, comms, resources), the way NASA JPL's Team X designs missions.
  3. Choose the orbit and the rocket. The dashboard keeps mass, power, money, data, communications and time in balance, and every gauge shows a sweet spot instead of "more is better".
  4. Pass a review board that uses JPL's concept maturity checklist.
  5. Run your own tests: vibration, thermal vacuum, deployment, radio and a day-in-the-life test. Each one finds one kind of hidden flaw. Skip it and that flaw flies with you.
  6. Launch, unfold, find the first signal, then fly years of operations. Problems arrive as telemetry, not answers, and you pick the fix.
  7. Read the report: a score out of 1000 with the reasons. Change one thing and fly again "with the same luck" to see what it did.

Six missions: First Light (a CubeSat tutorial), Angola from Above (Earth observation for crops, floods and the coast), Connecting Angola (a geostationary TV and internet satellite), Far Side Relay (Moon), Red Planet Orbiter (Mars) and Crew Around the Moon (a capsule modelled on Artemis II).

Five levels: Guided (a pointer shows the next click, made for people who know nothing about space), Cadet, Engineer, Expert and Sandbox.

Teams: five roles (Mission Director, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, Communications Lead, Resource Manager) shared by 1 to 4 players, on one screen or online with a room code. Every role has a secret goal that pulls against the others, so the team has to negotiate, and launch needs a GO from everyone.

Real science and NASA data: Kepler orbits, the sun-synchronous tilt from J2, eclipses, drag decay, ground-track coverage, link budgets with tropical rain fade, the rocket equation, launcher capacity, battery wear, life support per crew-day and radiation dose. How clear Angola's sky is comes from 13,482 Landsat 8 and 9 scenes (2021 to 2025), read through the Microsoft Planetary Computer: 61% clear over a year, but 38% in January and 86% in June. So a camera needs about twice the passes in the rainy season, and that's when radar wins. The Earth is NASA's Blue Marble, the stars are NASA's Deep Star Maps, and the constants come from NASA's GMAT. Every number carries its source in the code, and our own estimates are marked in the game.

Why it matters: in class, mission trade-offs stay abstract. Here you feel them. A lower orbit gives sharper pictures, but drag ends the mission sooner. A bigger antenna gets more data home, but costs mass and power. Skipping a test saves time, but the flaw can end the mission. Players learn how real teams work (start from the user, pass the reviews, test as you fly), and a whole class can play on one shared screen.

What's creative: nothing is prebuilt. The 3D spacecraft grows as you add parts, and the camera flies to whatever you just changed. Failures are telemetry puzzles. "Fly again with the same luck" makes every change a fair experiment. The paperwork (radio licence, debris assessment) is part of the engineering. The report ends with real missions like yours.

What we thought about: Angola's own space programme (GGPEN, who set the challenge), so the first missions serve Angola's farms, floods and coast. Players with no space background (the Guided level, plain words, a glossary). Classrooms with one screen or weak internet. Big readable text, and switches for sound and music.

Built with: TypeScript, React, three.js (React Three Fiber), zustand, Vite, and Vitest for the automated tests. All sound and music are made in the browser with Web Audio, so there are no sound files. A small Node.js server runs the online rooms. Hosted on Vercel and Render. Open source under the Apache License 2.0.

Links

Play: https://www.riwaspace.earth/

Online team rooms: https://space-underdogs.onrender.com/ (a free server, the first visit can take a minute)

AI use: The video in the presentation is a screen recording of the real game. Sound and music are made by code in the browser, not AI audio. There are no AI-generated images or video, and nothing AI-made uses NASA branding. Just the audio in demonstration youtube video is generated by AI.
